title: EU Gas Stocks Plunge to 15-Year Low as LNG Diverts to Asia; OPEC+ Holds October Quotas
subhead: The Iran war's cost is now hitting Europe's gas buffer hardest: EU storage has fallen to 65.5%, a 15-year low for this time of year, as US LNG diverts to higher-paying Asian buyers. Meanwhile OPEC+ held October output quotas unchanged and shifted focus to a 2027 baseline review, and Venezuela is weighing an OPEC exit as its production recovers.

sections.heading: EU Gas Storage at 15-Year Low as LNG Diverts to Asia
sections.body:
The clearest sign yet that the Iran war's energy shock is spreading beyond oil: EU natural gas storage has fallen to 65.5%, the lowest level for this time of year in 15 years, according to European Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data cited by the Financial Times. Stored volumes total about 742 terawatt-hours, more than 20% below the five-year average, per the Seoul Economic Daily's summary of the FT report.

The cause is a diversion of supply, not a collapse in demand. After the EU halted Russian pipeline gas, as much as 70% of US LNG exports went to Europe — a share that fell below 50% in June as Asian buyers, led by South Korea, outbid the bloc, Reuters reported. The Asian JKM benchmark stood at about $17.33 per million BTU, above Europe's $13.19. EU gas prices have risen about 75% over the past two months, touching 75.3 euros intraday on September 2, a three-year high. The EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators estimates filling storage would cost an extra 10-15 billion euros at 50 euros per MWh — and prices are now in the 70-euro range.

The European Commission insists there is no immediate crisis, betting on El Nino-driven mild weather and a 17% structural drop in EU gas consumption. But GIE head Lucie Boost warned that a single shock — an LNG supply disruption, a cold snap or lower renewables output — could worsen the situation, and a combination would be far worse.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's gas buffer is the war's quiet casualty. The bloc eased its 90% storage mandate to 80% in April betting the war would end; it hasn't, and now the buffer is thinner than at any point in 15 years heading into winter, with Asia outbidding Europe for LNG. This is the mechanism by which the Gulf conflict becomes a European heating and industrial crisis.

sections.heading: Iran-US Re-Escalation: Exclusion Zone Threat, Tanker Strikes, Oil Near $100
sections.body:
The fragile pause has collapsed into a new escalation cycle. Iran's new Supreme National Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tehran will announce an 'exclusion zone' outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, extending from the line of the US naval blockade into the Persian Gulf, Reuters and CBS reported. Iran separately threatened the US with 'economic warfare' and said it had fired an advanced missile at US warships, per Reuters.

On the US side, CENTCOM said it has redirected 94 commercial ships accused of violating the blockade on Iranian ports, disabled three and boarded two, CBS reported. CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Saturday's strikes 'permanently disabled' three Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for IRGC ballistic missiles fired at Navy ships, warning: 'If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.'

The market response is sharp. Brent hovered near $97-98 a barrel, WTI above $92, the highest since late July, with Brent up about 60% so far in 2026, Bloomberg reported. US regular gasoline averaged $4.14-4.15 a gallon, near a Labor Day record. Hormuz traffic fell to its lowest since May — 10 ships a day on average, with only two on Saturday and six on Sunday, per Kpler data cited by Reuters. Iran also raised gasoline prices for its heaviest users to 100,000 rials (about 7 cents) per liter, double the December rate, affecting 15% of consumers as record consumption of 145 million liters a day outpaces domestic production of 122 million.
sections.whyItMatters: The de-escalation window has closed. Iran is formalizing a maritime exclusion zone that would institutionalize control of the strait, while Washington is destroying the tankers that move Iran's oil revenue. With Hormuz transit at a fraction of normal and both sides escalating, the war premium is rebuilding — and Iran's own gasoline rationing shows the blockade is biting Tehran's domestic economy too.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Holds October Quotas, Shifts Focus to 2027 Baseline
sections.body:
OPEC+ chose stability over action. The alliance kept October oil production targets unchanged at 31.01 million bpd, with the seven producers — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — maintaining September output levels, according to a statement on OPEC's website reported by Rigzone and The Finance World. The group is pausing further adjustments while it reviews members' production capacity to set a 2027 output baseline, Astana Times and Leadership reported.

The decision comes as the cartel's market power is being tested from multiple directions: the Iran war has disrupted Gulf exports, China's buying behavior has become the real swing factor, and the UAE's April departure plus Venezuela's possible exit are eroding cohesion.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ is effectively standing pat while the war does the work of tightening the market. Holding quotas unchanged with Brent near $100 signals the group sees no need to add barrels — and its focus on a 2027 baseline review suggests it is planning for a post-war world rather than reacting to the current disruption.

sections.heading: Venezuela Weighs OPEC Exit as Output Recovers
sections.body:
Venezuela is in internal deliberations over leaving OPEC, according to a Kpler analysis reported by Safety4Sea — months after the UAE's April departure and amid rising friction from Iraq. Venezuelan production has risen from about 700,000 bpd in January to roughly 1.2 million bpd, though it remains far below historical levels and is guided toward only about 1.4 million bpd by late 2027, keeping Caracas within its OPEC quota exemption for the next two to three years.

Kpler's Homayoun Falakshahi called an exit 'structurally likely' but not imminent. A Venezuelan departure alongside the UAE would remove roughly 6 million bpd of production capacity, about 20% of OPEC's total. The analysis notes Venezuelan barrels are already moving largely outside OPEC's supply-management logic: US Gulf Coast exports exceeded 700,000 bpd in July, India has returned as a buyer of Merey and Boscan grades, and the ARA region received its first Venezuelan cargo in seven years. Domestic politics — acting president Delcy Rodriguez's tilt toward Washington and internal Chavismo opposition — may be the bigger swing factor than oil-market logic.
sections.whyItMatters: Venezuela's production recovery, driven by the US-backed investment push, is quietly decoupling it from OPEC's discipline. A founding member leaving — on top of the UAE — would hollow out the cartel further, even if the near-term price impact is limited because Venezuelan output is already quota-exempt.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Prepares Broader IAEA Oversight as Nuclear Diplomacy Intensifies
sections.body:
Nuclear diplomacy is moving on two fronts. IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi said Saudi Arabia is preparing to grant the agency more intrusive verification and monitoring powers under its planned civil nuclear program, Reuters reported — though the planned US-Saudi atomic deal does not include Riyadh signing the Additional Protocol, the gold-standard safeguards instrument. Separately, Grossi said there is 'no engagement' with Iran on resuming inspections of its nuclear facilities, with Tehran indicating it will not cooperate until a broader political agreement is reached, CBS reported. The US is proposing that Iran be referred to the UN Security Council over nuclear non-compliance, per Bloomberg.

Grossi also revealed that a near-complete nuclear reactor built secretly during Assad's rule in Syria would have been able to produce weapons-usable material when Israeli jets destroyed it in 2007, Reuters reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The Gulf war is accelerating a nuclear realignment: Washington is deepening its atomic partnership with Riyadh even as it turns the diplomatic screws on Tehran. Saudi Arabia's willingness to accept broader IAEA oversight — short of the Additional Protocol — is the price of the US civilian nuclear deal, while Iran's refusal to re-engage leaves the inspection regime in limbo.

sections.heading: China's Crude Buying Rebounds, Tightening the Market
sections.body:
The demand side of the oil equation is shifting. Chinese crude buying has returned to the market, driving up prices of barrels from West Africa to Canada in recent days, Bloomberg reported, after Beijing's buying hiatus earlier in the war was a key factor quelling prices. Chinese seaborne imports ticked up in August from July but remained nearly 40% below pre-war levels, Reuters noted, while Shanghai crude futures pushed above $100 as demand surged, per CryptoBriefing.

The rebound is amplifying the supply shock. Hedge funds have turned the most bullish on Brent since May, with net-long wagers on US crude at their highest since June, Bloomberg reported. Energy Aspects' Amrita Sen said the pace of inventory drawdowns 'has accelerated so much in crude just over the last couple of weeks' and that crude is 'poised to take a significant leg higher.'
sections.whyItMatters: China was the shock absorber that kept oil below $100 — its reserve cushion and buying hiatus blunted the war premium. With Beijing returning to the market just as Gulf exports are squeezed, the two forces that were offsetting each other are now aligning, which is why analysts see Brent testing $100 and Goldman Sachs warning of $120 in an escalation scenario.

sections.heading: India Targets Colombia's Critical Minerals and Oil
sections.body:
New Delhi is diversifying its energy and mineral supply chains into South America. India's KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India) and ONGC Videsh are stepping up engagement with Colombia as India seeks to diversify mineral supplies and crude imports, StratNewsGlobal reported. The push comes as India's oil and gas sector is squeezed by high crude and LNG prices driven by the Iran war, per OilPrice.com.

The move reflects a broader pattern of non-Western buyers locking in supply relationships outside the disrupted Gulf and Red Sea routes, and of India hedging its dependence on Middle East crude at a moment when Hormuz transit is unreliable.
sections.whyItMatters: India is quietly building alternative supply relationships in Latin America — both for crude and for the critical minerals needed in its energy transition. It is a reminder that the war's disruption is pushing major importers to diversify away from the Gulf, reshaping long-term trade flows even as the conflict dominates headlines.

bottomLine: The Iran war's energy shock is now hitting Europe's gas buffer hardest: EU storage at 65.5% is a 15-year low for this time of year, as US LNG diverts to higher-paying Asian buyers and the bloc's eased storage mandate leaves it exposed heading into winter. Meanwhile the US-Iran conflict has re-escalated — Iran plans a Hormuz exclusion zone, Washington has disabled three Iranian tankers and redirected 94 ships, and Brent is back near $98 with Goldman Sachs warning of $120 in an escalation scenario. Beneath the price action, OPEC+ held October quotas unchanged and shifted focus to a 2027 baseline review, Venezuela is weighing an OPEC exit as its output recovers, and China's return to crude buying is tightening a market that its earlier hiatus had helped calm. The through-line: the war's costs are spreading from crude into gas and refined products, and the market's shock absorbers — China's reserves, OPEC's spare capacity, Europe's storage — are all running thinner.
sources: Reuters, CBS News, Bloomberg, Financial Times (via Seoul Economic Daily), GIE, Kpler, Rigzone, The Finance World, Astana Times, Leadership, Safety4Sea, OilPrice.com, StratNewsGlobal, CryptoBriefing, World Oil, Forbes, Energy Aspects, Goldman Sachs, IAEA
